Field surveys of White River spinedace (Lepidomeda albivallis) in the upper White River system have provided key insights into the species' maximum body size. The ultimate total length attained by adults reaches approximately 15 centimeters [Li = approximately 15 centimeters], a modest dimension typical of small-bodied cyprinids adapted to cool, spring-fed desert streams. This measurement, derived from extensive seine-net sampling over multiple seasons, places Lepidomeda albivallis among the smaller members of the western spinedace group. In comparison with the closely related Lepidomeda mollispinis, which can exceed 18 centimeters in total length, the White River spinedace appears constrained by the narrower thermal and trophic conditions of its isolated spring habitat. Males and females exhibit minimal dimorphism in ultimate size, a pattern consistent with monogamous or pair-spawning reproductive behavior. Estimates of standard length from preserved museum specimens corroborate the field data, confirming that individuals rarely surpass this 15-centimeter threshold (15 centimeters) [Li = 15 centimeters] even in the most productive reaches of their remaining range. These morphological limits are critical for understanding the species' overall life-history strategy and energetic demands.

Reproductive development in White River spinedace follows a relatively compressed schedule, with puberty occurring at a total length of approximately 7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7 centimeters], based on fork length conversions from 6.5 centimeters. At this size, juveniles transition into the reproductively active adult phase, exhibiting fully developed gonads and the capacity for spawning. Field collections indicate that most individuals attain this pubertal length by their second spring, though growth rates vary with local thermal regimes and food availability. The small size at which sexual maturation is achieved suggests an opportunistic life-history strategy, allowing the species to reproduce even under conditions of high adult mortality or unpredictable resource pulses. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from captured specimens reveals that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis commence promptly upon reaching the 7-centimeter total length (7 centimeters) [Lp = 7 centimeters], with no evidence of a prolonged adolescent period. This early onset of reproductive capability is common among cyprinids inhabiting harsh desert environments, where maximizing lifetime fecundity requires rapid maturation.

At the stable thermal conditions of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], which characterize the spring-fed headwaters this species depends upon, the age at first reproduction has been estimated at approximately 2 years, corresponding to a total length of roughly 108 millimeters. Under these same cool temperatures, females exhibit continuous batch spawning over an extended breeding season; each female produces approximately 6.85 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 6.85 eggs per spawning event] when measured at a standard length of 92 millimeters, with multiple events across the season [F_R_i = multiple events across the season]. This per-event fecundity is relatively high for a fish of this body size and underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover in its isolated spring environment. The 13 °C thermal regime is critical, as metabolic rates and oocyte development are tightly coupled to water temperature in this stenothermic fish. Reproduction occurs primarily during the late spring and early summer months, with females releasing multiple small clutches over several weeks. The combination of moderate longevity and moderate per-event egg output suggests an iteroparous strategy that buffers against occasional recruitment failures in the unpredictable desert stream environment.

Egg dimensions provide important information regarding maternal investment and offspring quality. Based on data from the congeneric species Lepidomeda aliciae, the wet weight at birth for newly hatched yolk-sac larvae is approximately 0.0048 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0048 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of 2.1 millimeters from which they emerge. This modest neonatal mass is characteristic of small-bodied cyprinids that produce large numbers of relatively tiny offspring rather than a few large ones. In contrast, the estimated wet weight at maturation for an adult female reaching the ultimate total length of 15 centimeters is substantially greater, calculated from length-weight regressions at 35.4 grams [Wwi = 35.4 grams]. This nearly ten-thousand-fold increase from larval mass to adult body size underscores the rapid growth trajectory typical of short-lived desert fishes. The exponential nature of the length-weight relationship, with an exponent of approximately 3.06, indicates that larger individuals are disproportionately heavier, a pattern observed across many cyprinid taxa. The small larval mass also implies high dependence on exogenous food sources immediately following yolk absorption.

At the size of puberty, estimated at 7 centimeters total length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 3.65 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.65 grams], as derived from the same length-weight relationship. This intermediate body mass represents the point at which individuals have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support gonadal development and the metabolic costs of spawning. The threefold difference between the 3.65-gram pubertal mass (3.65 grams) [Wwp = 3.65 grams] and the species' ultimate adult mass of 35.4 grams [Wwi = 35.4 grams] illustrates the substantial scope for post-pubertal growth in this species. Regarding lifespan, the maximum longevity under natural conditions, when water temperatures remain consistently at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], has been estimated at approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years]. This lifespan is relatively extended for such a small-bodied fish and likely reflects the stable, low-temperature environment of the spring-fed habitat, which slows metabolic aging. However, field recapture data suggest that most individuals in wild populations do not exceed 5 to 8 years due to predation and episodic habitat disturbance.
